item.title: Himuka / Hyuga Coast Scenic Drive — Guide
item.description: Miyazaki’s coastline offers superb scenic driving not only south along the Nichinan Coast but also north around the Hyuga area, where the dramatic ‘Himuka’ coast features some of the prefecture’s most striking sea scenery. The star attraction is Cape Umagase (Umagase), where sheer cliffs of columnar volcanic rock — formed by ancient lava flows and eroded into remarkable regular pillars — drop dramatically into the deep blue sea, viewed from clifftop walkways and lookouts.

item.title: Nanatsugama Sea Caves — Guide
item.description: Nanatsugama, meaning ‘seven cauldrons’, is a striking natural formation on the rugged Genkai Sea coast near Yobuko and Karatsu in northern Saga. Here the relentless waves of the Genkai Sea have carved a series of seven deep sea caves into a wall of towering basalt cliffs, their vertical columns of volcanic rock and cavern mouths creating a dramatic, elemental seascape. From the clifftop above there is a lookout with sweeping coastal views and a small shrine, while in calm weather sightseeing boats sail right up to and even into the largest caves, letting you feel their scale from the water.

item.title: Sanriku Ria Coast: Iwate's Dramatic Pacific Shore — Guide
item.description: The Sanriku coast’s dramatic ria shoreline — where mountains plunge straight into the Pacific — forms one of Japan’s most spectacular coastal landscapes. Sea arches, basalt stacks and hidden coves stretch some 200 km from Miyako to the Aomori border, best explored by sightseeing boat or on the scenic Sanriku Railway. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sanriku coast, Iwate Hours Always accessible; boats daytime Admission Free; boat/rail fares apply Time needed Half day+ Best time Late spring–autumn (calm seas) What to See Dramatic ria cliffs where mountains meet the sea.

item.title: Cape Hedo Guide: Okinawa's Northern Tip, Cliffs & Access
item.description: Cape Hedo (Hedo Misaki) is the wild northernmost point of Okinawa’s main island, where rugged limestone cliffs meet the deep blue of the open sea. A windswept viewpoint with crashing waves below, it offers sweeping panoramas and, on clear days, a glimpse of distant Yoron and Okinoerabu islands to the north. The cape also carries historical weight: a monument here commemorates Okinawa’s 1972 reversion to Japan. Paired with the karst formations of nearby Daisekirinzan and the Yanbaru forest, it’s the grand finale of a northern road trip.
